title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
description: Reconstruct a queue from height and in-front-count constraints, using a greedy sort-tallest-first-then-insert strategy.

blocks.text: Given an array people where people[i] = [h, k], h is a person's height and k is the number of people in front of them who have height >= h, reconstruct and return the queue as an array satisfying every person's k value.

blocks.caption: Placing people tallest-first, at their exact required index, means later shorter insertions never disturb already-satisfied taller placements.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","people[][] (each [h, k])"],["k meaning","Number of people in front with height >= this person's height"],["Output","A valid queue ordering satisfying every person's k value"]]}

blocks.text: Processing people from TALLEST to shortest and inserting each at index k in the growing result list is the key greedy insight: since every already-placed person is at least as tall, a new (shorter) person's k value directly tells their EXACT position, and inserting them there never invalidates any already-placed taller person's count (a shorter person behind them, wherever inserted, never counts toward their "people in front with height >= mine" requirement).

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This "process from the most constrained/dominant element down, inserting directly at the required position" pattern is a classic greedy-with-insertion technique for constraint-satisfaction reconstruction problems.

Picture building a lineup by inserting the tallest people first. Once someone is placed, only EQUALLY tall or taller people placed later can affect their k count, since shorter people inserted anywhere never count toward "people at least as tall in front of me." Sorting tallest first and inserting each person directly at their required index guarantees every constraint is satisfied by construction.

blocks.caption: Shorter people inserted later never disturb the counts of already-placed taller people.

items: Sort people by height descending; for equal heights, sort by k ascending (so among equally tall people, the one requiring fewer "at least as tall" people in front is placed first).
Insert each person, in this sorted order, at index k in the result list.
Since every already-placed person is at least as tall, a new person's k directly determines their correct final index.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The final queue is [[5,0],[7,0],[5,2],[6,1],[4,4],[7,1]], matching the expected output exactly.

A direct approach repeatedly selects the tallest remaining person (breaking ties by smallest k) and inserts them at their required index, removing them from the remaining pool each time. This directly implements the greedy rule but rescans the remaining pool for the tallest person on every step.

Sorting everyone once up front, by height descending then k ascending, produces the exact same processing order without any repeated rescanning, since the sorted order already reflects "tallest, and among ties, fewest required people in front" at every step.
Repeatedly find the tallest remaining person (breaking ties by smallest k), insert them at their required index, and remove them from the remaining pool.

codes.python:
def reconstruct_queue(people):
    n = len(people)
    result = []
    remaining = list(people)

    while remaining:
        tallest = max(remaining, key=lambda p: p[0])
        candidates = [p for p in remaining if p[0] == tallest[0]]
        candidates.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])
        chosen = candidates[0]
        result.insert(chosen[1], chosen)
        remaining.remove(chosen)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(reconstruct_queue([[7, 0], [4, 4], [7, 1], [5, 0], [6, 1], [5, 2]]))

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","Each of n insertions rescans the remaining pool for the tallest person"],["Space","O(n)","The result and remaining lists"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Rescanning the remaining pool for the tallest person on every step is unnecessary once everyone is pre-sorted in the correct processing order.
Sort everyone once by height descending, then by k ascending for ties. Insert each person, in this sorted order, at index k in the growing result list.

items: Sort by (height descending, k ascending), O(n log n).
Insert each person at index k in the result list, in sorted order.
Each insertion into a list costs O(n) in the worst case (shifting later elements), for O(n^2) total, but with no rescanning needed to find the next person to place.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, repeated rescan for tallest","O(n^2)","O(n)"],["Optimized, sort once then insert","O(n^2)","O(n)"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Both share O(n^2) overall due to list insertion cost, but the optimized version removes the O(n) rescan per step, replacing it with a single O(n log n) sort up front.

items: Processing elements from most-constrained (tallest) to least-constrained (shortest) and inserting directly at their required position is a powerful greedy reconstruction technique.
The key correctness insight: once sorted by height descending, a later (shorter) insertion can never invalidate an earlier (taller) person's already-satisfied count.
This "insert at the constraint-given index, processed in dominance order" pattern generalizes to other reconstruction-from-relative-constraints problems.

blocks.text: Queue Reconstruction by Height is solved by sorting people by height descending (ties broken by k ascending), then inserting each person at index k in the growing result list. Since taller people are always placed first, later insertions of shorter people never disturb their already-satisfied counts, giving a correct reconstruction in O(n^2) time.
